title: Saving the School Garden
subtitle: Use evidence to help a community garden grow
summary: The school garden dries out during warm weeks. Listen to the garden team, read two kinds of evidence, choose a fair next step, explain your plan aloud, and write a recommendation for the principal.

briefing.scene: The school garden is healthy after rain, but some beds dry out before the next watering day. Your team has been asked to study the evidence and recommend one change that will help plants without wasting water.
briefing.goal: Use a detail from the garden notes and a number from the water test to explain your recommendation.

dispatch.title: A message from the garden team

turns.speaker: Ms. Lee
turns.text: Our garden gets water on Monday and Thursday. The sunny bean bed feels dry by Wednesday afternoon, but the shady lettuce bed is still damp.

turns.speaker: Mateo
turns.text: We tested two ways to cover the soil. The uncovered tray lost more water than the tray with dry leaves on top. We should compare the numbers before we choose.

turns.speaker: Ms. Lee
turns.text: We have enough dry leaves for two beds. A neighbor can bring straw next month, but we do not know how much. The team needs a plan we can try this week.

report.title: What a soil cover can do
text: Water can leave soil and enter the air. This is called evaporation. On a warm, sunny day, uncovered soil may lose water faster than soil protected by a cover. A layer of dry leaves or straw is called mulch. Mulch shades the soil and slows evaporation, so more water can stay near plant roots.

Mulch does not make extra water. Gardeners still need to check the soil and water plants when they need it. A cover that is too thick can press on small stems, so it should leave room around each plant. Different beds may need different care: a sunny bed can dry sooner than a shady bed.

tasks.q: The team has leaves for two beds. Which plan best uses the evidence and notices a limit?

options.text: Cover all six beds deeply and stop checking the soil, since the test proves mulch makes water.
Stop watering every bed because mulch makes water for plants.

tasks.explain: Leaves kept the most water in the test, and there are enough for two beds. Checking soil matters because mulch slows evaporation but does not make water.

phases.title: Choose a plan to test
phases.instructions: Use the listening notes, science passage, and table. Pick a first step the school can actually try this week.

decision.q: What should the garden team try first?

options.label: Put a light layer of dry leaves on two sunny beds and check the soil before watering.
options.consequence: This uses the leaves available now and focuses on beds that dry sooner.

options.label: Cover every bed deeply and stop checking the soil.
options.consequence: This ignores the limited supply and the report's advice to keep checking plants.

guided.model: I would cover two sunny beds first because the garden team has enough dry leaves for two beds. Mulch can slow evaporation, so water may stay near the plant roots longer. In the test, the tray with dry leaves had 78 milliliters left, while the uncovered tray had 54 milliliters left. The test supports trying leaves, but the team should still check the soil before watering. That way, the team can see whether the plan helps the sunny beds.

phases.title: Recommend a garden change
phases.instructions: Write a short recommendation for the principal. State a first step, support it with evidence, explain why the evidence matters, and include one way to check the plan.

task.title: Write to the principal
task.scenario: The principal wants a short, evidence-based plan the garden team can try this week.
task.prompt: Write a recommendation for the garden. Name which beds to cover first, use one number from the test, explain what mulch does, and tell how the team can check whether the plan helps.

Mulch shades the soil and slows evaporation, so more water may stay near the roots. The team should check the soil on Wednesday and note whether the covered beds are still damp. This small trial uses the leaves we have and helps us decide what to do next.
